entries.title: India's 'cockroaches' vs Election Commission: What you need to know ahead of CJP's October 10 protests
entries.summary: The Indian capital New Delhi has been turned into a fortress with train and metro cancelations, barricades and heavy police presence ahead of Saturday's planned protests against the chief of India's electoral body.
entries.content:
India

Why are India's 'cockroaches' protesting again?

October 9, 2026

The Indian capital New Delhi has been turned into a fortress with train and metro cancelations, barricades and heavy police presence ahead of Saturday's planned protests against the chief of India's electoral body.

India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called for a nationwide march on New Delhi on Saturday, after its ultimatum demanding the resignation of the country's election chief was ignored.

In the days leading up to the planned gathering, authorities have been clamping down on protesters gathering at Jantar Mantar, the 18th-century observatory that serves as the Indian capital's designated protest site. 

These include the general public, student activists and leaders of opposition, including the Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke urged people to turn out in huge numbers, while adding that the Delhi police were already detaining protesters: "The more people you detain, the more people will show up!"

The stakes remain high: the credibility of the body that runs the world's largest elections is on the line.

What is the controversy about?

Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is currently in the hot seat after the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that revealed that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) acted against the written advice of the two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

Kumar became the chief election commissioner (CEC) in 2025 after being chosen by a selection panel led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Rahul Gandhi, who was also a member of the panel, had opposed Kumar's appointment.

Now, Kumar, along with Sandhu and Joshi, is responsible for overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), a nationwide re-verification of the electoral rolls requiring voters to prove their eligibility to remain on them.

The ECI says the process is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls, including deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved abroad and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."

But critics say it has gone far beyond that remit.

The Indian Express report says more than 130 million names were removed from electoral rolls across the country. For scale, Germany has about 60 million eligible voters in total.

Who are the 'cockroaches' and what do they want?

A play on the name of Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the youth-led movement emerged in May after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark during an unrelated court hearing.

The move backfired, with young people embracing the tag and turning it into an avenue for disillusionment over what they see as failings in the country's education system and its massive youth unemployment problem.

The CJP has amassed nearly 25 million Instagram followers, more than double that of the BJP's 9.9 million. Modi, however, remains far ahead at 106 million.

A campaign protesting multiple competitive exam leaks launched the CJP into nationwide relevance, securing the resignation of the then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Now, the CJP is demanding:

  • Kumar's resignation and initiation of criminal proceedings against him
  • An immediate hold on upcoming elections, and freezing the SIR
  • The repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India

Is CJP really leading the protests?

The CJP is not alone in its call for protests.

For days ahead of the planned October 10 march to Jantar Mantar, student activists, civil society members — including former high-ranking government officials — and leaders of opposition have been taking to the streets of Delhi calling for accountability and Kumar's resignation.

The CJP was joined by representatives of several student associations, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star Neha Bora, who has been leading protests in the capital all week.

Meanwhile, dramatic scenes emerged from New Delhi as leaders from the opposition INDIA alliance, including the Gandhis, were detained repeatedly by authorities as they took to the streets calling for Kumar's resignation.

Bharatiya Kisan Union spokesperson and farmer rights activist Rakesh Tikait also extended his support to the march and vowed to join on October 10. Tikait was part of the leadership  behind the 2020-2021 farmers' agitation, which forced the Indian government to repeal three laws intended to liberalize the agricultural sector.

The other side

Amid heavy police presence and barricading near the ECI offices in lush central Delhi, the electoral body has rejected any suggestion of a split and Kumar's overreach, maintaining that all decisions, including on the SIR, were unanimous.

It also addressed allegations that opposition parties were not allowed to meet with its officials on Tuesday, saying that till "4.00 pm today, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with the Election Commission."

A day earlier, a delegation of retired senior bureaucrats had also attempted to approach the office of the ECI to submit a charge sheet and impeachment notice against Kumar on behalf of the public, but were unable to reach the premises.

Delhi police said no permission has been given for the October 10 protests, calling it illegal.

"I request everyone to refrain from participating in this protest," Delhi's Deputy Commissioner of Police Shrishti Pandey told news agency ANI.

Some BJP politicians had previously referred to the CJP as a "cross-border influence operation" aimed at destabilizing India, with federal minister Kiren Rijiju accusing them of seeking social media followers ⁠from archenemy Pakistan and the "anti-India gang."

What to watch for on October 10

New Delhi has been turned into a fortress, with the government deploying close to 43,000 security personnel ahead of the protests, local media reported.

Several independent journalists and others associated with the last round of CJP protests have claimed that authorities have been using intimidation tactics to keep them from joining the march. 

Among those arrested is CJP national spokesperson Deepak Baliyan, who was taken into police custody on Thursday, but released hours later.

In the last round of CJP protests, the police had used tear gas, sticks and pellet-firing shotguns to subdue the demonstrators.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Hurricane Isaias intensifies en route to US Gulf Coast
entries.summary: Oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has already been affected by the approaching hurricane, which has strengthened so far to Category 2.
entries.content:
United States of America

Hurricane Isaias intensifies en route to US Gulf Coast

October 9, 2026

Oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has already been affected by the approaching hurricane, which has strengthened so far to Category 2.

Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall over the US Gulf Coast, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday. The storm's approach coud disrupt oil and gas production.

Isaias has been forecasted to cross the coast in either Florida, Alabama or Mississippi on Friday night or early Saturday.

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for coastal areas in four counties in northeastern Florida, while states of emergency are in place in parts of neighboring Alabama and Georgia.

"Isaias will be a dangerous hurricane with significant storm surge, damaging winds, and flooding rains when it reaches the northern Gulf Coast," the NHC said.

The NHC urged residents that emergency preparations to protect lives and property from high winds and storm surges "should be rushed to completion."

First Atlantic hurricane this year

Isaias has strengthened to a Category 2 storm over the Gulf of Mexico, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of the Mississippi River delta, packing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph).

The hurricane is the very first to develop in the Atlantic this season, which began June 1.

The remarkably quiet hurricane season was caused partly due to a strong El Nino weather phenomenon. It causes strong vertical wind shear — dry air and sinking air over the Atlantic Ocean —, hampering storm formation and intensification in the area.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal authorities would coordinate response efforts with state and local governments.

"To everyone in the storm's path: ask that you also do your part to stand ready. Now is the time to prepare," Mullin said on X.

Storm impacts oil and gas production

The path of the storm covers some important industry points of oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico. As a result, platforms and rigs were already evacuated.

Some 63% of the oil production in the region has been temporarily suspended, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).

Similarly, some 57% of gas production has also been suspended, the MMA said.

Offshore production in the Gulf accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

Hurricane Simon heads for Pacific

Meanwhile, the Pacific Ocean has been affected differently by the El Nino phenomenon.

El Nino's effect has left little vertical wind shear over the Pacific, creating favorable conditions for hurricanes to intensify. This has caused this year's Pacific hurricane season to be more severe than usual.

Hurricane Simon is currently moving toward Mexico's Pacific coast, with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, the NHC said.

The storm has reached Category 1 and has been forecasted to reach Jalisco state, where the popular tourist resort of Puerto Vallarta is located, on Friday night or early Saturday, the NHC says.

"Rapid intensification is expected to continue, and Simon is expected to be a very dangerous major hurricane when it approaches the coast of Mexico," the NHC said.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?
entries.summary: Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

World Cup: Is Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium a concern?

October 9, 2026

Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111 miles) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.

Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general re-evaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing.  The draw-back from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."

Priorities changing, with sports losing out

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multi-billion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.

Parallels between Qatar 2022 and Saudi Arabia 2034

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry has responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.

"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a Fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.

"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames."

Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."

World Cup will still matter to Saudi Arabia

But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.

"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.

Gulf Cup hosting a postivie sign before Asian Cup test

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.

Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions.”

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: France: Investigators recover 2 stolen Renoir paintings
entries.summary: Thieves had initially taken four pieces with a value of over $10 million, but dropped two as they fled. Officials praised everyone that tracked down the paintings, but didn't reveal how they found them.
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

Thieves had initially taken four pieces with a value of over $10 million, but dropped two as they fled. Officials praised everyone that tracked down the paintings, but didn't reveal how they found them.

Two Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in France last month have been found, authorities said on Friday.

Police have arrested six people in connection with the crime.

The two stolen paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the Renoir Museum is located. "Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."

The heist followed a string of high-profile robberies from European museums, including the theft of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris last year.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Voting to begin in local elections in the Czech Republic
entries.summary: The vote is being seen as a test of popularity for the Andrej Babis government.
entries.content:
Czech Republic

Voting to begin in Czech local, Senate elections

October 9, 2026

The vote is being seen as a test of popularity for the Andrej Babis government.

Voters in the Czech Republic begin casting ballots in local polls on Friday to elect local representatives as well as one-third of the Senate's members.

The elections are being seen as a test of popularity for the populist billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

Babis took power last December after forming a coalition with two small political groups. His party, the ANO, or YES, won big in parliamentary elections last year after he was able to tap into people's economic frustration, playing into a sentiment that the center-right government at that time was spending too much on Ukraine.

But Babis ran into challenges as well after having formed a government, with the opposition challenging his widening budget deficit — which is when the government spends more than it earns. But he survived a no-confidence vote in parliament earlier this month.

Babis, 72, founded the Patriots for Europe in the European Parliament with former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and other far-right parties. 

Housing shortage is big issue in Czech cities

More than 8 million eligible voters are set to elect municipal and town councils in more than 6,200 districts nationwide.

Housing shortages, a big theme in major European cities including Berlin and Madrid, is a top concern for voters in the Czech Republic's major cities too.

As for the Senate, a third of the seats are up for grabs, as they are every two years.

The vote will determine whether the liberal and conservative opposition can retain their majority in the chamber or whether the governing parties and their allies make gains.

President Petr Pavel drew attention ahead of the vote because he said he was not going to be able to cast his ballot since he was on a private holiday outside Europe.

"The president regrets the planning error," his spokesman said.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: South Africa pulls asylum directive after violent protests
entries.summary: South Africa has withdrawn a controversial asylum directive after anti-migrant protests descended into violence and chaos on Thursday.
entries.content:
South Africa

South Africa pulls asylum directive after violent protests

Published October 8, 2026last updated October 9, 2026

South Africa has withdrawn a controversial asylum directive after anti-migrant protests descended into violence and chaos on Thursday.

South Africa has halted a new directive for the processing of asylum applications after violent protests broke out in Johannesburg and Durban.

The directive was issued by the Department of Home Affairs in response to a court judgment.

The court had ruled that asylum seekers could not be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Offices for asylum seekers were quickly overwhelmed, and that placed officers at serious risk, the Department of Home Affairs said.

That's because the court ruling led to days of protests in the major coastal city of Durban, which then spread to Johannesburg's Soweto township on Thursday.

Rioters torched 14 cars in Durban and 10 in Soweto. Shops were looted in both locations.

What else do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. Vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

What is the court ruling that sparked protests?

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."

Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa: What to know

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amid international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Germany women's football team: Can Ena Mahmutovic make a case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper?
entries.summary: The women's friendlies against Australia and Japan present an opportunity for Ena Mahmutovic to make her case for succeeding Ann-Katrin Berger as Germany's first-choice goalkeeper.
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

The women's friendlies against Australia and Japan present an opportunity for Ena Mahmutovic to make her case for succeeding Ann-Katrin Berger as Germany's first-choice goalkeeper.

Having qualified for next summer's World Cup in Brazil, the German women's national team is wrapping up this year's schedule with friendlies against Australia this Friday and Japan next Tuesday, and the choice of opponents was deliberate.

"Their style of play isn't what we're used to in Europe. That's what I want to prepare my team for," Germany coach Christian Wück said.

"These will be high-level matches, and they will challenge us in a completely different way than European teams do."

Wück said that his team had built a "solid foundation" over the past few years and that now it was all about taking the "next step" in their development.

"We are looking to continue along this path and refine it," he said.

"We know our strengths, but we need to utilize them 100% against top teams if we are going to hold our own," sporting director Nia Künzer said.

Can Mahmutovic seize her chance in goal?

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women is also a hot topic.

The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League, where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.

Parallels to men's goalkeeping situation

This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, is set to get her chance to shine.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück told the prematch press conference in Karlsruhe on Thursday.

"We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country.

The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.

For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.

'The future of the national team'

"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said with a view to the upcoming friendlies.

"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."

Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.

Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.

"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

Costly mistake in Germany debut

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.

Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.

"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.

Unusual Bundesliga debut

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.

"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."

That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.

"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.

Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti
entries.summary: The new leader of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be elected on October 10. The reis-ul-ulema's role is not only important for Muslims in the country itself, but could inspire Muslims across Europe.
entries.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina

Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti

October 9, 2026

The new leader of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be elected on October 10. The reis-ul-ulema's role is not only important for Muslims in the country itself, but could inspire Muslims across Europe.

The reis-ul-ulema or Grand Mufti of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the head of the country's Islamic community, represents the interests of Muslims before the state, expresses himself on political, moral and social issues and defends the independence of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina against attempts at foreign influence.

Having served two seven-year terms, the current Grand Mufti, Husein Kavazovic, is no longer permitted to run.

Three candidates are competing to become his successor: Salem Dedovic, the Mufti of Mostar, Nedzad Grabus, the Mufti of Sarajevo, and Mensur Malkic, the head of the Directorate for Religious Affairs of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Grand Mufti's envoy.

While Malkic's focus lies in strengthening the Islamic Community in religious and institutional terms, Dedovic has stated that he sees the office in a more political light and would like it to become more engaged in social debates. Grabus, who has the most international experience as the former Grand Mufti of Slovenia, says he would like to strengthen the community in times of globalization and secularization. 

"No other Islamic personality in Europe holds a position like the Reis-ul-ulema in Sarajevo," said Imam Benjamin Idriz, the head of the Islamic Community in the Bavarian city of Penzberg and the chair of the Munich Forum for Islam. "That's why the importance of this election extends far beyond the country, to Muslims and non-Muslims alike, across Europe."

The President of the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Germany (IGBD), Zenahir Mrakovic, said that the "election is important to us, because historically, theologically and institutionally, we share close ties with the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

"Bosniak" is the name Bosnian Muslims use for themselves. With around 100 communities across the country, the IGBD is one of Germany's smaller Muslim associations.

Muslims have lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina for centuries. Islam was introduced to the population when to Ottoman Empire spread through southeastern Europe. The organizational structure of the Islamic Communities was established after the Berlin Congress in 1878, which, among other things, placed Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian rule.

Following the example of Christian churches, the Austro-Hungarian rulers soon officially recognized Islam as a religious community and in 1882, they founded the Council of Ulema and appointed the first Reis-ul-ulema as president.

Unique self-organization of the Muslim faith

This kind of Islamic self-organization could become a model for Muslims across Europe. The Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina is independent from the state and is financed with donations, membership fees and zakat, a form of charity given by Muslims.

The Islamic Community has its own sort of parliament, the Sabor, and a Constitutional Court that ensures the community's actions are in line with the constitution of the country in which it operates. The Riyaset is the community's highest executive body, responsible for implementing decisions. Its headquarters are in Sarajevo.

In the 150 years since its founding, the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina has survived numerous political upheavals and repeatedly adapted to new circumstances. After the Ottoman Empire came the Habsburg monarchy and Austro-Hungarian rule, then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito. Following Tito's death, the Bosnian War for independence ended in 1995 with the Dayton Accords.

Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a secular state with a democratic constitutional order. Time and again, the Islamic Community has clearly distanced itself from radical tendencies. It has a history of cooperation and coexistence with Jewish and Christian communities.

This has also left an impression on the roughly 400,000 Bosnian Muslims living in Germany.

"In the process of institutionalizing Islam in Germany, the experience of the Bosniaks' Islamic Community should be taken more strongly into account," said Esnaf Begic, a former imam and a lecturer at the Institute for Islamic Theology at Osnabrück University. "We are autochthonous European Muslims and to a certain extent, we share more similarities with Germans than with Muslims from Afghanistan, Iran or Saudi Arabia."

Mrakovic, head of the IGBD, agrees that Bosnia's experience with organizing religious life in a democratic and pluralistic society could also be useful to other Muslim communities. "It's not about telling other people how to live their Islamic faith but about learning from our own experiences: how we preserve our religious identity while remaining a natural part of European, democratic society.

An office in challenging times

The new head of Bosnian Muslims will be assuming his role in challenging times. Statehood in Bosnia and Herzegovina remains fragile, and foreign actors are vying for more influence. "Attempts to exert more influence aren't only coming from Ankara or Riyah, but also from Washington, Berlin or Brussels. They, too are, trying to act upon the Reis-ul-ulema in their own interest," Begic said.

In Europe, anti-Muslim racism and Islamophobia have reached levels that are becoming increasingly frightening for Muslims. Right-wing populists are on the rise, and extremist parties are attracting more and more supporters bent on denying Muslims the right to participate in society.

Given the circumstances, the new Reis-ul-ulema will be expected to employ the full democratic and historical legitimacy of his office to actively engage in debates about Islam in Europe.

This is what Idriz, the imam from Penzberg, hopes for, too. He believes the new Reis-ul-ulema could inspire more confidence not only in Bosniaks, but in all European Muslims, while signaling to majority societies that Islam is a part of Europe, and that it affirms and embraces values such as the rule of law, gender equality and freedom of expression. "In the future, the Reis-ul-ulema should lay an even stronger emphasis on this," Idriz said.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Finland: The world's happiest country has a debt problem it can no longer ignore
entries.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years. 

With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.

Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic

Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.

EU scrutiny over growing deficit

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.

"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.

Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.

National Coalition rules out tax hikes

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.

While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.

Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.

With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion

Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.

"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

Markets give Helsinki time to reform

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.

That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: Nobel Peace Prize 2026 goes to Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law
entries.summary: South African judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won this year's Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Follow DW live.
entries.content:
Published October 9, 2026last updated October 9, 2026

South African judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won this year's Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Follow DW live.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
  • The Peace Prize committee praised the South African's commitment to international justice
  • The prize has been awarded 106 times to 143 laureates between 1901 and 2025
  • It carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (around $1.2 million; €1 million)
  • This week, Nobel laureates have already been named in medicine, physics, chemistry, and literature.

Below is all the news and views, previews and reviews surrounding the award of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

Skip next section Germany congratulates Pillay on Nobel prize

Germany congratulates Pillay on Nobel prize

The German government paid its tribute to Navi Pillay shortly after the announcement of her award.

Pillay's work fighting against apartheid and for human rights, justice and international law deserves the "highest respect," government spokesman Steffen Meyer said in Berlin.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Pillay "stood for the idea that peace is grounded in justice."

He went on to praise her for her verdicts at the ICJ concerning the genocide in Rwanda and her work as head of the UN human rights commission.

Awarding her the Nobel Peace Prize not only honored her own work, but was also an "important commitment to international criminal justice."

Skip next section South African president celebrates Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize

South African president celebrates Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has congratulated jurist Navi Pillay on winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, describing the award as a tribute to her lifelong commitment to justice, peace and human dignity.

"She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place," Ramaphosa said in a statement issued by his office.

He praised Pillay's pioneering work as a defense lawyer for anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, and her subsequent career in international justice.

Pillay went on to serve as a judge and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and later as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

She currently serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.

South Africa has itself brought a separate case before the ICJ, accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention through its military campaign in Gaza. Israel rejects the allegations.

"Justice Pillay's crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally," Ramaphosa said.

He noted that Pillay joins fellow South African Nobel Peace Prize laureates Albert Luthuli, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and former President Frederik Willem de Klerk.

Skip next section Israel condemns Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay

Israel condemns Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay

Israel's Foreign Ministry has sharply criticized the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, accusing her of spreading false allegations against Israel.

"If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner," the ministry said in a statement.

It accused Pillay of the "politically motivated demonization of Israel" and promoting what it called the "genoLIE," a reference to allegations that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.

Pillay previously chaired a UN commission of inquiry that concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The commission is among a growing number of international bodies, human rights organizations and genocide scholars to reach that conclusion. They include Amnesty International, Israeli rights groups B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights Israel, and the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

Israel rejects the genocide allegations. The International Court of Justice is examining a case brought by South Africa but has not yet issued a final ruling.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry said awarding Pillay the prize amounted to the "grotesque weaponization" of the Nobel Peace Prize to legitimize anti-Israel prejudice.

Skip next section EU chief hails Pillay as 'defender of the persecuted'

EU chief hails Pillay as 'defender of the persecuted'

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has praised Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay as a champion of international justice who has confronted some of humanity's darkest chapters.

"Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did," von der Leyen wrote on X, congratulating the South African lawyer and human rights activist.

She highlighted Pillay's work confronting injustice, from apartheid in South Africa to the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

"She has looked the brutality of injustice in the eye and never looked away," von der Leyen said.

"She is the defender of the persecuted, the vulnerable, the voiceless and the excluded. Of the rule of law over the right of might," she wrote.

"In a world that needs justice more than ever, her courage and moral clarity are a precious compass," the EU chief added.

Skip next section Pillay jokes about sharing award with Trump

Pillay jokes about sharing award with Trump

South African jurist Navi Pillay has joked that she might share her Nobel Peace Prize with US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly made clear his desire to win the prestigious award.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," Pillay said as she received applause in Nuremberg, Germany, after being announced as this year's winner.

Trump has claimed to have ended eight wars and argued that his diplomatic achievements merit a Nobel Peace Prize. Some of the conflicts he cites were not full-scale wars, while the extent of his role in resolving others has been disputed.

The US president has also suggested that denying him the award would be an insult to the United States, although he has acknowledged that the Norwegian Nobel Committee might not select him.

Skip next section UN welcomes Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay

UN welcomes Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay

The United Nations has welcomed the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, saying it highlights the growing importance of human rights.

"It's wonderful to see this being awarded to Navi Pillay, the former High Commissioner for Human Rights," said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.

"It is testament to the need and to the value of human rights in this world more than ever," she added.

Skip next section Amnesty hails Pillay Nobel Peace Prize as 'inspired choice'

Amnesty hails Pillay Nobel Peace Prize as 'inspired choice'

Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard has welcomed the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, calling it "such a great and inspired choice."

Callamard praised Pillay's longstanding commitment to international law and justice, saying the award came at a particularly critical moment.

"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she wrote on X. "Congratulations dear Navi," she added.



Callamard was with Pillay at the Nuremberg courthouse in Germany when the award was announced.

"We are at the Nuremberg Court; I cannot think of a stronger symbol for her Nobel prize," Callamard wrote on X. "We are all so thrilled!"

Nuremberg was the site of the historic trials of leading Nazis after World War II, which helped lay the foundations of modern international criminal law.

Skip next section Nobel committee warns against rule of the strong

Nobel committee warns against rule of the strong

Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jorgen Watne Frydnes has warned of a dangerous shift towards a world in which might takes precedence over right, as he announced the Nobel Peace Prize for South African jurist Navi Pillay.

"Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence," Frydnes said, after praising Pillay's decades of work to strengthen international law.

He warned that the international legal order was facing an increasingly serious challenge, with powerful countries often escaping accountability for their actions.

"We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice," he said.

Frydnes acknowledged that the rules-based international order had never been perfect.

"The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim," he said.

"Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms rather than threats, violence and warfare."

The central lesson, he said, was that lasting peace must rest on legal principles rather than "the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power."

Skip next section Nobel committee praises Pillay's role in international justice

Nobel committee praises Pillay's role in international justice

Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jorgen Watne Frydnes praised Navi Pillay's contribution to international justice, saying:

"The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who, with exceptional courage and integrity, has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order."

"This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted," he said.

Frydnes also highlighted Pillay's lifelong commitment to justice.

"Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and a firm moral compass have been constants in a long career."

He also noted her early experiences under apartheid.

"Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion," the committee chair said.

Frydnes drew a connection between her early activism and her later international judicial work.

"A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time."

He said that Pillay had "significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law."

Skip next section Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay

Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay

South African human rights lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

Born in 1941 in Durban, Pillay grew up under apartheid and became one of South Africa's first women of Indian descent to practice law. She defended anti-apartheid activists, including fellow Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nelson Mandela, and fought to end discriminatory prison conditions.

After apartheid, she became a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she helped establish landmark legal precedents recognizing rape as an act of genocide. She later served as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014.

More recently, she chaired a UN commission investigating human rights violations in Israel and the Palestinian territories.



Skip next section The 2026 Nobel winners

The 2026 Nobel winners

This week, laureates have already been named in medicine, physics, chemistry, and literature. The Nobel week will conclude on Monday with the announcement of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

The winners of this year's Nobel prizes

Medicine: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries that provide new insights into how we might treat blindness, depression, addiction and dementia. 

Physics: Francis Halzen for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and discovery of high-energy neutrinos, described as "ghostly messengers from space."

Chemistry: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

Literature: Anne Carson for her "bold and inventive oeuvre" that combines the classical with the modern.

Skip next section Nobel Peace Prize: The winners forced to stay away

Nobel Peace Prize: The winners forced to stay away

Maria Corina Machado was unable to accept her Nobel Peace Prize in person last year. But the Venezuelan is not the only winner unable to attend the ceremony, with incarceration a common historical thread.

Here are some of the other most notable absentees.

Skip next section The 2025 laureate Maria Corina Machado ... and Donald Trump

The 2025 laureate Maria Corina Machado ... and Donald Trump

The recipient of last year’s prize was Maria Corina Machado for "her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela." 

However, she was unable to collect the award herself in the December ceremony as the ruling Socialist government in Caracas warned she would make herself a fugitive if she "fled" Venezuela.

Machado's daughter Ana Corina Sosa Machado accepted the Nobel Peace Prize on her behalf and delivered remarks that her mother had written for the occasion.

"It reminds the world that democracy is essential to peace," read the remarks. "And the most important lesson Venezuelans can share with the world is a lesson forged on a long and difficult path: If we want democracy, we must be prepared to fight for freedom."

Machado then gave her medal to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought Washington's support for her efforts.

Trump said just this week that he was "very honored to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history ‌deserves it more than President Trump."

Skip next section Controversial Nobel Peace Prize winners

Controversial Nobel Peace Prize winners

From Yasser Arafat to the UN: Why did they receive a Nobel Peace Prize? It's a question asked almost every year in Oslo. Criticism of the award is as old as the prize itself.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — The curse of Nobelitis

IN DEPTH — The curse of Nobelitis

After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense.

They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

Read our analysis of what happens when winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur.
